A1.justification: Both PDFs describe revisions of the same inversion-based memorization study, despite the changed title and substantial redesign. All text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. Inspection covered all 14 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including v2's supplementary Sections 7–10; v1 has no separate appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original replication-recognition experiments, prompt and noise inversion experiments, and quantitative memorization measurements on Stable Diffusion and an FFHQ model (Sections 4–6).

after.justification: v2 reports original detection results, controlled training-factor experiments, membership comparisons, and extensive inversion ablations across four datasets, including supplementary results.

M1.justification: v1's separate prompt inversion and Wasserstein comparison against an assumed-safe unconditional model are replaced by InvMM: minimizing inverted-noise KL divergence subject to replication. v2 adds adaptive regularization and stopping, plus joint categorical prompt-distribution inversion using Gumbel-Softmax (Section 4, Algorithm 1). Gaussian noise regularization and reconstruction-error optimization already existed in v1; their integration and the resulting measure change substantially.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates LAION images and an FFHQ model. v2 retains these datasets and adds CIFAR-10 and CelebAHQ, a suspicious LAION population with highly duplicated images not replicated by their training captions, and member-versus-hold-out evaluation. This substantially broadens the represented data and evaluation tasks.

E2.justification: v1 Table 1 compares tiled-l2, SSCD, and reconstruction-error replication recognition. v2 Table 1 instead evaluates training-loss metrics, MLOO, and Wen's detector against InvMM. SecMI is added in Figure 9, and GBDA participates in the supplementary prompt comparison. AutoPrompt and PEZ remain evaluated; SSCD remains as a replication criterion rather than a comparison-table baseline.

E3.justification: The evaluation is substantially redesigned. v1 uses 7,800 generated image/noise/prompt tuples and a 78-memorized/100-normal image study; v2's detection cohorts contain 99 positive and 1,000 negative CIFAR-10 images, and 76 confirmed and 50 normal LAION images. New protocols control training epochs across dataset sizes, manipulate duplication, evaluate SD v2.1, and apply SSCD-based stopping with manual CIFAR-10 corrections (Sections 5 and 8).

E4.justification: v1 mainly investigates regularization, token counts, and selected hard-prompt failures. v2 adds adaptive-weight comparisons, temperature/discretization and CFG sweeps, reconstruction-versus-noise objective ablations, controlled training-duration and duplication studies, nearest-neighbor consistency checks, and membership error analyses (Sections 5.2–5.5 and 8–9). These provide substantial new evidence about mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v1's KS normality tests at a 0.05 threshold and p-value distributions averaged over 1,000 samples are removed, eliminating its principal hypothesis-testing component. Its best-of-up-to-20 initialization reporting for hard-prompt inversion also disappears with that procedure. v2 instead specifies that MLOO uses ten-fold cross-validation conducted once (Section 8.2). Neither version provides systematic repeated-seed uncertainty for headline performance.

E6.justification: The Wasserstein measurements and replication-recognition results are replaced by InvMM results and new analyses. v2 Table 1 reports InvMM AUC/TPR@1%FPR of 0.997/0.899 on CIFAR-10 and 0.994/0.842 on SD v1.4. v1's reconstruction-error recognizer reports 0.999/0.986 at sample level under a different task and cohort, so these are not comparable performance deltas. v2 also adds training-factor trends, Table 3's consistency results, and three newly uncovered suspicious LAION replications (Section 9.8).

T1.justification: v1's three-condition definition and Wasserstein/Chebyshev rationale are replaced by a formal sensitivity function, sensitivity-constrained KL minimization, and entropy-based reasoning (v2 Equations 8–11). Supplementary Section 7.1 adds a conditional variational lower-bound formulation involving noise and condition distributions. These are substantive mathematical changes, although the Gaussian KL formula and reconstruction/noise-loss relationship are retained.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from three-condition security analysis and comparison with a safe unconditional reference to InvMM and its adaptive estimator. v2 foregrounds measurement across unconditional and text-guided models, analysis of training factors, and the distinction between memorization and membership. Image-based analysis without collected prompts remains a shared claim, while v1's safe-reference/Wasserstein contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning training duration, duplication, and the gap between perceptual replication and membership inference. It replaces v1's unconditional-model safety rationale and explicitly discusses Gaussian modeling limitations, SSCD failures, and dependence of invertibility on settings. The existing soft-versus-hard prompt limitation is retained and developed through temperature and discretization evidence (Sections 6, 8.2, and 9).

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code access link, an NVIDIA A800 hardware disclosure, and Table 2's dataset-specific optimization, sampling, stopping, and SSCD-resolution settings. Its supplement documents baseline implementation and manual calibration procedures beyond v1's shorter experimental settings. Conversely, v1's explicit starting-noise alignment prescription is not retained; its omission alone does not establish an actual sampling change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around membership inference, latent-recovery measures, memorization factors, and inversion-based detection and copyright applications, with corresponding new citations. The retained van den Burg work receives a stronger cross-dataset comparability critique, and Section 5.4 challenges confounding between dataset size and training epochs in earlier studies. Several derivative-generation safety discussions and citations from v1 are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and concluding narrative are extensively rewritten. v1's separate recognition, triggering, and measurement sections are reorganized into a unified method section and experiment section. Related work moves near the beginning, and a new supplement organizes technical derivations, detailed experiments, prompt ablations, and additional generations.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is extensively rebuilt: new inversion and sensitivity schematics, training-factor and membership plots, redesigned prompt-comparison panels, and large supplementary generation grids replace or expand v1's displays. Table 1 changes its comparison structure, and hyperparameter and consistency tables are added. Typography, the title block, and main-text/supplement layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 provides substantially stronger validation of the measurement approach through controlled regularization, training-duration, and duplication experiments, addressing v1's limited testing of its estimator and reliance on an assumed-safe reference model. The supplement makes implementation and failure conditions much more assessable. Manual CIFAR-10 score corrections, relaxed prompts, and missing repeated-seed uncertainty still limit the conclusions, but the improved validation and explicit applicability limits constitute a substantial net quality gain.
